parole.significato: A supernatural being similar to an elf; one of the Dǫkkálfar or Ljósalfar.
parole.testo: From Danish and Swedish alf, from Old Norse alfr; see also Dutch alf. Doublet of elf, awf, and oaf.

parole.significato: A county in Denmark.
parole.testo: From Danish amt.

parole.significato: A Danish cheese made from sour buttermilk.
parole.testo: From Danish appetitost: appetit (“appetite”) + ost (“cheese”).

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: From Danish atten (“eighteen”), with reference to the (negative) exponent in the relevant power of ten; the same principle also explains femto-.

parole.significato: A kind of steelyard used in Orkney.
parole.testo: From Danish bismer, from Middle Low German bisemer, via a Slavic language from Turkish batman (“a unit of weight”).

parole.significato: Any low perennial plant whose buds overwinter just above soil level
parole.testo: From Danish kamæfyt, chamæfyt, equivalent to chamae- (“ground”) + -phyte (“plant”) (first element from Ancient Greek χαμαί (khamaí, “on the ground”)).

parole.significato: A variety of Havarti cheese made from highly pasteurized milk.
parole.testo: Partial calque of Danish flødehavarti.

parole.significato: A semi-soft, aged cow's milk cheese originating in Denmark, where it is a common household cheese.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish Danbo.

parole.significato: Danish.
parole.testo: From Danish dansk, Swedish dansk, Icelandic dansk.

parole.significato: A Dane.
parole.testo: From Danish dansker.

parole.significato: To run quickly or for a short distance.
parole.testo: From Middle English daschen, dassen, from Danish daske (“to slap, strike”), related to Swedish daska (“to smack, slap, spank”), of obscure origin. Compare German tatschen (“to grope, paw”), Old English dwǣsċan (“to quell, put out, destroy, extinguish”). See also dush.

parole.significato: The field of computer science.
parole.testo: From data + -logy, from Danish datalogi. Proposed for use in English by Danish scientist Peter Naur.

parole.significato: A northern bottlenose whale (Hyperoodon ampullatus), from which oil was once obtained.
parole.testo: From a typographical variant of Danish døgling, from Faroese døglingur, which now refers to the northern bottlenose whale (Hyperoodon ampullatus).

parole.significato: A padded blanket used as a cover in bed; a duvet.
parole.testo: Originally a product name, derived from Danish dyne /dyːnə/. Trademark owned by the Tontine Group.

parole.significato: elle-people
parole.testo: From Danish ellefolk.

parole.significato: A type of elf of Scandinavian folklore.
parole.testo: Calque of Danish ellefolk.

parole.significato: All the shared body of knowledge which is not explicitly used when people communicate, but without which communication…
parole.testo: From Danish eksformation, or from explicitly discarded information.

parole.significato: Faroese, of or pertaining to the Faroe Islands, Faroese people, and/or Faroese language.
parole.testo: From Danish Færø and Faroese Føroyar.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: From Danish femten (“fifteen”), with reference to the (negative) exponent in the relevant power of ten; the same principle also explains atto-.

parole.significato: A rocky, barren plateau, especially in Scandinavia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish fjeld. Doublet of fell.

parole.significato: To strip the blubber or skin from, as from a whale, seal, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish flense (now spelled flænse).

parole.significato: One who flenses (cuts blubber from a whale carcass)
parole.testo: From Danish flense or Dutch vlensen, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *flintaz-, from Proto-Indo-European *splind- (“to split, cleave”), from *(s)plei- (“to split”)..

parole.significato: An oblate-spheroid meatball of North European origin, eaten hot or cold, and typically consisting of: minced pork or be…
parole.testo: From the Danish frikadelle and its etymon, the German Frikadelle. Doublet of fricandeau and frikkadel.

parole.significato: To lead.
parole.testo: From Danish føre, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną. Cognate with Dutch voeren (“to lead”), Low German fören (“to lead”), German führen (“to lead”), Luxembourgish féieren (“to lead”), Icelandic færa (“to move, carry, convey”), Faroese føra (“to lead, carry”), Swedish föra (“to lead, guide, steer, direct

parole.significato: A program or algorithm that downloads images or media from a web site that have not been publicly linked, based on gues…
parole.testo: From Danish fusker (“a person covertly doing work outside official guilds”).

parole.significato: Excessive activity, worry, bother, or talk about something.
parole.testo: Of unknown origin. Perhaps from Danish fjas (“nonsense”), from Middle Low German (compare German faseln (“to maunder, talk nonsense”)). Compare also fouse (“to hasten, rush, tumble, disarrange”).

parole.significato: A brief, aphoristic poem, often containing irony or paradox.
parole.testo: From Danish gruk, coined by the Danish poet Piet Hein.

parole.significato: A semi-soft Danish cow's milk cheese.
parole.testo: From Danish havarti. Named in 1952 after Havartigården near Holte, where the Danish cheese pioneer Hanne Nielsen worked in the 19th century.

parole.significato: A type of mermaid of Danish folklore.
parole.testo: From Danish havfrue.

parole.significato: A three-legged supernatural horse associated with death or Hel in Danish folklore.
parole.testo: From Danish helhest.

parole.significato: Any plant whose buds rest on the surface, being protected in various ways.
parole.testo: From Danish hemikryptofyt, equivalent to hemi- (“half”) + cryptophyte, from crypto- (“hidden”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: A feeling of cosiness, comfort, contentment and conviviality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish hygge, Norwegian Nynorsk hygge or Norwegian Bokmål hygge.

parole.significato: A middle-aged white woman who exhibits a strong sense of white privilege and entitlement—often rooted in racism against…
parole.testo: From Danish Karen, a vernacular form of Catherine that arose in medieval Denmark. The sense "middle-aged woman" comes from the popularity of the name among baby boomers and Gen-Xers. The derogatory usage was popularized via African-American Vernacular English.

parole.significato: A cake constructed from a stack of rings of decreasing diameter, each made of marzipan, egg whites and sugar.
parole.testo: From Danish kransekage.

parole.significato: A Scandinavian pastry, a variety of pretzel.
parole.testo: From Danish kringle, ultimately from Old Norse kringla (“ring, circle”).

parole.significato: The currency of Iceland, Denmark (including Greenland and the Faroe Islands) and Norway, divided into 100 øre, except i…
parole.testo: From Danish krone (“crown”) and Norwegian krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, krona, and króna.

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-dipyramidal violet pink mineral containing calcium, hydrogen, manganese, oxygen, silicon, and sodium.
parole.testo: From Kvanefjeld + -ite. From Danish Kvanefjeld, a compound of kvan (“garden angelica”) + -e- + fjeld (“mountain”). Its namesake is the locality of the mineral.

parole.significato: The occupation of land, especially if previously uncultivated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish landnam, from Old Norse landnám. Compare Dutch landname and German Landnahme.

parole.significato: Any of several small, coloured, plastic bricks, often made by the Lego Company, that can be made to join together and b…
parole.testo: Name of a company founded in 1934, shortened from Danish leg godt (literally “play well”). Coincidentally, the word also means “I put together” in Latin (see legō).

parole.significato: A small arctic and subarctic rodent of the tribes Lemmini, Dicrostonychini and Lagurini.
parole.testo: From Danish and Norwegian lemming, from Old Norse lómundr, læmingi, læmingr (“lemming”), perhaps from Sami luomek. Sense 2 derives from a longstanding myth that they exhibit so much herd mentality that populations jump off cliffs to their deaths together.

parole.significato: A Scandinavian food made from coarsely ground pork liver and lard, seasoned and baked.
parole.testo: From Danish leverpostej.

parole.significato: A long natural blowing horn without finger holes, played by embouchure.
parole.testo: From Danish lur, Norwegian lur, and Swedish lur, all from Old Norse lúðr (“trumpet”).

parole.significato: Friable forest humus that forms a layer of mixed organic matter and mineral soil and merges gradually into the mineral…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish muld, from Old Norse mold.

parole.significato: A fabric creation technique predating knitting and crochet, involving passing the full length of the working thread thr…
parole.testo: From Danish nålebinding, literally "needle-binding," from nål + binde.

parole.significato: A shapeshifting water spirit in Germanic mythology and folklore; a nix.
parole.testo: From Danish nøkke, Swedish näck.

parole.significato: A nix; a hobgoblin, especially one that resides in a farm house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish nisse.

parole.significato: A prehistoric bronze axe of the middle Bronze Age with a thin haft for a forked handle and a thick blade.
parole.testo: From Danish paalstav.

parole.significato: The scientific study of kissing.
parole.testo: From Danish filematologi, from Ancient Greek φῐ́λημᾰ (phĭ́lēmă, “a kiss”) + ologi (equivalent to English -ology), but compare the New Latin philēmatologiā, which appears written in Greek as φιληματολογία in the title of a 1659 book.

parole.significato: A group of German families who settled in the heathlands of central Jutland in Denmark during the mid-1700s.
parole.testo: Calque of Danish Kartoffeltyskere, in reference to the cultivation of potatoes in the areas they settled.

parole.significato: The discontinuous change of the state of an electron in an atom or molecule from one energy level to another.
parole.testo: Possibly calque of Danish kvantespring.

parole.significato: A pastry filling or topping made from butter creamed with sugar and often including marzipan or some form of almonds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish remonce, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: In seal engraving, a small metal disc at the end of a tool.
parole.testo: From Danish [Term?] (“a groove”). Compare rifle (“to score, to make grooves”) and the past participle riflet (“scored, grooved, rifled”), riffeln with the same meaning. Also see rifle (“a rifled gun”).

parole.significato: A bird, the ptarmigan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish rype.

parole.significato: To drink the entire contents of a drinking vessel without pausing.
parole.testo: See skull. The verb sense may derive from Danish/Norwegian/Swedish skål.

parole.significato: Synonym of nautical mile, a unit of distance now equal to exactly 1852 meters
parole.testo: As a former Scandinavian unit of distance, a calque of Danish sømil, Norwegian Bokmål sjømil, and Swedish sjömil, from Danish sø (“sea, nautical, maritime”) + mil (“Danish mile or league”).

parole.significato: Discontinuation, especially of a psychoactive drug.
parole.testo: From Danish seponering (“discontinuation”), + -ation.

parole.significato: To smile in a foolish, frivolous, self-conscious, coy, obsequious, or smug manner.
parole.testo: Uncertain; compare (probably from) Danish simper / semper (“coy”), German zimper (“elegant, dainty”).

parole.significato: A scoundrel.
parole.testo: From Danish skælm, from Middle Low German; cognate to German Schelm.

parole.significato: A Scandinavian monetary unit and coin up to the 19th century. (A subdivision of the Swedish riksdaler, the Danish and N…
parole.testo: From Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish skilling. Doublet of shilling.

parole.significato: A toast when drinking, roughly equivalent to cheers.
parole.testo: From Danish/Norwegian/Swedish skål, which is used when making a toast and also means "bowl".

parole.significato: A drinking-toast; cheers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish skål.

parole.significato: An open-faced sandwich that usually consists of a piece of buttered rye bread, topped with commercial or homemade cold…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish smørrebrød.

parole.significato: A Viking fighting vessel smaller than a longship
parole.testo: From Danish snekke, from Old Norse snekkja, probably from Proto-Germanic *snakkǭ, *snakkaz, related to Old English snacc (“swift sailing vessel”).

parole.significato: Synonym of gossip mirror.
parole.testo: Calque of Danish gadespejl.

parole.significato: a phenomenon of most Danish dialects, in which stressed long vowels or consonants are laryngealised in certain contexts…
parole.testo: From Danish stød.

parole.significato: A variety of small, roundish carrot that does not need to be peeled.
parole.testo: From thumb, as a calque of Danish Tommelise, the original name created by Hans Christian Andersen.

parole.significato: A troll.
parole.testo: From Danish trold.

parole.significato: A young person who is ugly, but who is expected to become beautiful or handsome as they mature.
parole.testo: Calque of Danish grim ælling. From the fairy tale of a duckling, considered ugly, that matures into a magnificent swan.

parole.significato: Any of several related fat-soluble vitamins, found in leafy green vegetables, essential for blood clotting.
parole.testo: Named similarly to the other vitamins, that are named after their order of discovery. This one was assigned its "K" from Danish koagulation by the Danish researcher Henrik Dam. The sense that is a slang alias for ketamine is because of the initial letter of that drug's name, as also with the slang s

parole.significato: To do a clumsy or inelegant job, usually as a temporary repair; mend, patch up, repair.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bocchen (“to mend, patch up, repair”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle Dutch botsen, butsen, boetsen (“to repair, patch”) (Dutch botsen (“to strike, beat, knock together”)), related to Old High German bōzan (“to beat”), See beat; or perhaps from Old English bōt

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A thick cloud that forms near the ground; the obscurity of such a cloud.
parole.testo: Origin uncertain; but probably of North Germanic origin. parole.significato: To hum or sing (a tune) at a low pitch or volume.
parole.testo: Possibly either: * a blend of Shetland Scots nune (“to sing softly, croon, hum”) (from Danish nynne, Norwegian nuna, nynna (“to hum; to sing”), originally imitative) + English doodle (“to play the bagpipes”) (chiefly Scotland); or * from Norn (unattested), from Old Norse *grynta, from Proto-Germanic

parole.significato: Thanks.
parole.testo: Uncertain, but possibly young child's pronunciation of thanks. Alternatively, derived from Danish tak, from Old Norse þǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz.
